articles.body:
一面铜镜的正面用于照容，背面却能成为容纳异域图像的小天地。这件唐代镜以狮形兽和葡萄藤为主要母题，馆方将两者视作来自中国以外的装饰元素。镜背的动物与枝蔓不是随便点缀，而是理解当时富裕阶层审美的一条线索。

唐代同类镜式的流行，显示器物工艺与跨地域文化往来并行。观看时可以顺着枝蔓寻找动物位置，理解自然形态如何被组织成密集而有节奏的装饰。它的吸引力不依靠虚构法术，而在于普通照容用具也保存着开放的时代趣味。

“海兽葡萄纹”是推荐名称，具体兽种仍不强定。纹样来源能支持交流背景，却不能证明本件在海外制造，更不能据此推定墓主人或完整流传路线。

两只类似豹的动物环绕镜钮，仿佛彼此追逐；外圈文字却转向一位女子照镜的意象。馆方将这种自然化动物造型放在隋唐时期的变化中，强调它与更早紧密整合的镜背装饰有所不同。

动物的紧张动势和诗句中的细腻人物形成对照，使小小镜背同时容纳图像和文字。它值得展示的地方在于这种双重表达，而不只是“古镜”这一笼统标签。观看顺序可以从镜钮走向双兽，再沿外圈理解诗意，不需要为镜子补造一个传奇主人。

兽名与诗文译读还需专业核对。图鉴只概述馆方解释，不擅自添加铭文作者、写作事件或未记录的使用者。

圆鼓的壶腹上，金色线条与卷曲纹、交错兽纹一起铺开。这件战国酒器的特殊之处在错金：馆方描述青铜表面先形成凹部，再嵌入金，使两种金属在器身上形成鲜明对照。

它也显示青铜器意义的变化。馆方认为此时某些酒器已不只是礼仪用品，更能表现拥有者的财富和身份。连续曲线顺着圆腹伸展，让工艺与器形互相增强；玩家可以在这一过程中理解装饰为什么不只是附加图案。

社会身份的解释适用于机构提供的背景，不能由华丽程度确定本件主人。未记录的酒液、宴会地点、制作者与使用经历都继续未知，游戏价值也另属策划提案。

钩喙鸟立在纠缠的蛇龙之上，金银镶嵌又贯穿这个小型青铜构件的多个面。馆方把它与车辆、兵器及高身份者用品的装饰传统联系起来。精巧的器物并不一定是独立摆件，也可能是较大结构的一部分。

它最有趣的特点是可从各面观看的设计：立体动物组织轮廓，嵌饰强化表面细节。图鉴采用较宽的“饰端”，避免在装配关系尚未核定时直接称作某种车轴或兵器。用于展示时，可把器物组合中的“局部也有艺术”作为阅读主题。

鸟与蛇龙的力量关系是造型解释，不是实际战斗事件。具体装配位置、拥有者与出土背景都应回到机构证据，不能因凶猛纹样编造战争故事。

articles.body:
这件兽面构件原来衔着门环，门上实用部件因而有了弯角、凸眼、卷须与火焰状毛发。馆方将它解释为门饰和叩门构件，并讨论怪兽造型威慑侵入者、驱退恶灵的历史含义。

铺首值得收藏和展示，是因为功能与图像没有分开：兽口和悬环相连，观者可以理解装饰怎样服务建筑。鎏金还使复杂表面具有不同于普通木门的视觉效果。阅读时先认识衔环结构，再看面容，比直接套用一个神兽名字更稳妥。

驱邪是当时信仰的解释，不是现实功效。记录未明确原门、建筑或使用者，图鉴不会将它复原成某座确定墓门，也不补写缺失的门环样式。

articles.body:
四个跪姿人物围绕构件，身体也带装饰。馆方将它解释为大型建鼓的顶部提柄，配合悬置鼓体、从侧面演奏的使用方式。看似小巧的铜件由此与更大的音乐活动联系起来。

关于建鼓的认识不只来自孤立外观，还来自同类构件和墓葬乐器组合的比较。玩家可以注意人物排列与握持、悬挂功能怎样结合。展示时，这种“从附件认识乐器”的思路比把它当成无名铜像更有价值，也能介绍考古比较如何帮助解释器物。

馆方讨论的身体装饰和地方习俗联系属于解释。其他墓葬的发现不能代替本件出土记录，人物也不能直接认作已经确定族群和姓名的四位演奏者。

articles.body: 本篇以1941.549号馆藏为依据。器刃上方有眼耳突出的鸮首，使一件兵器形制的物品带有强烈的动物意象。馆方明确说，其用于仪式还是实际战争尚不清楚，驱邪意义也只是可能的解释。图鉴因此把形状与材质作为确定信息，把用途留作讨论。它适合提醒玩家：看起来像武器不等于已经证实参加过战斗，凶猛的装饰也不能代替使用痕迹和出土语境的证据。中文名称与解释为待审订稿，具体信息可由原始机构链接复核。
本篇以1942.1083号馆藏为依据。这对凤鸟由薄金片制成，细部经加工表现，沿边缘排列的小孔是理解用途的关键。馆方认为小孔暗示它们可能缝在织物上，因此原文名称保留问号。玩家可以比较成对构图与孔的位置，理解贵金属装饰怎样依附柔软材料。图鉴不将其直接定名为衣冠制度中的某种标准佩饰，也不因为是唐代金饰就推定来自皇室。中文名称与解释为待审订稿，具体信息可由原始机构链接复核。
本篇以1942.1083.1号馆藏为依据。这件单体凤鸟金饰的边缘留有细孔，馆方据此提出缝附织物的可能性。薄片成形与表面细部共同塑造鸟的轮廓，说明装饰效果不一定依靠厚重金属。这里的“织物饰”只是待审订功能译名，原文也带疑问号。其价值在于留下了连接方式的线索；具体缝在什么衣物、由谁佩戴，当前资料并没有回答。中文名称与解释为待审订稿，具体信息可由原始机构链接复核。
本篇以1944.61.b号馆藏为依据。本记录对应壶的盖部，不能在数据库中当作一件完整壶的同义名称。馆方介绍整器上的鸟形和几何龙纹，并讨论盖倒置后可作杯的解释。盖与器身的关系让玩家理解馆藏既可能按组合也可能按部件登记。图鉴保留这些层级，不凭共享介绍把不同馆藏号合并；酒宴与祭仪用途仍需结合整器资料，而非只靠一片盖判断。中文名称与解释为待审订稿，具体信息可由原始机构链接复核。
本篇以1947.3号馆藏为依据。矩形承接部逐渐收束为细长兽颈，银线和银带又组成卷曲、盘绕与交错的纹样。这件构件显示兵器附件也能有精细装饰，功能形制与视觉设计并不互斥。图鉴沿用馆方“弩支承构件”的解释，但不把它扩展为完整弩机的复原图。装配位置、实际使用方式与具体型号需要专门研究，现有记录只支持对器形与错银装饰的介绍。中文名称与解释为待审订稿，具体信息可由原始机构链接复核。
本篇以1951.151号馆藏为依据。这件酒器在中部突出牛首和角，口部向外张开，向下延伸的棱饰进一步增强器身的力度。馆方将它放在周人延续礼仪与铸铜传统的背景中，说明王朝变化并不等于器物传统突然消失。玩家可比较立体兽首和器身结构如何结合。图鉴不补写没有记录的祭祀过程，也不把装饰动物解释成某个历史家族的徽记。中文名称与解释为待审订稿，具体信息可由原始机构链接复核。
本篇以1951.292号馆藏为依据。镜背嵌入的银饰经过从背面锤起、正面细刻和小圆印冲压等加工。禽兽与枝叶形成高低变化，背景的细点又强化了质感。馆方对这类小镜用于儿童随葬或妇女妆台提出不同解释，因此尺寸小不应直接等同随葬专用。图鉴的重点是金属加工层次，并保留用途争议，不替器物选择一个看似动人的主人故事。中文名称与解释为待审订稿，具体信息可由原始机构链接复核。

articles.body:
鼎有承托器腹的足，是商代礼仪中盛放供食的重要器类。馆方把成组、大小不同的鼎与向祖先供献谷物和肉食的仪式联系起来，使器形、食物与社会秩序进入同一观察范围。

这件器物的知识价值还延伸到后世。古代青铜器长期被收藏、编目，铭文、形制与名称成为金石和古史研究的材料。玩家可以先辨认器形，再理解为什么礼器不仅属于它被制造的时代，也影响后来人认识过去的方法。

图鉴说明的是来源支持的用途与研究背景，不提供缺乏证据的具体祭祀日期、墓主人或铭文全文。三足结构只是识别起点，不能代替专业器型与年代核对。

这件爵在馆方说明中是用于祭献酒液的酒器。商代酒器的名称与形制彼此关联，爵、斝、觚等并不是可以互换的词。理解器类，比把所有青铜容器统称“酒杯”更接近历史使用语境。

它适合与鼎等盛食礼器一起展示：酒与食物都能进入祖先礼仪，但器物形式和操作方式不同。玩家可把承托、器口和使用姿态作为阅读线索，同时认识礼器怎样承载政治与信仰秩序。其吸引力来自可比较的类型知识，而非虚构诅咒。

机构解释支持祭献用途的范围，却不等于本件每一次使用都已知。所盛酒液、具体仪式与原拥有者没有记录就保持未知，正文不会添入未经核对的铭文或人物。

杯口有三条龙攀附，外壁可见寿字，淡色玉材与细致雕刻一起构成清代奢侈用品的视觉语言。馆方把龙纹、吉祥表达和高等级消费联系起来，使器物既有饮用形制，也有可观看的象征装饰。

它尤其适合介绍名匠归属的谨慎。来源曾讨论陆子冈名号，但没有把关联自动当成亲作证明。玩家可观察龙如何成为杯口与把手附近的形体，再理解名号、收藏趣味和市场需求为何会影响器物解释。

推荐名称依据器形与图像，不宣称官方中文命名。具体作者、作坊与拥有者仍待核验；“寿”所表达的是历史祝愿，不是玉杯具有延长寿命的科学证据。
本篇以1941.594号馆藏为依据。玉料被雕成山水与仙境的缩景，使一块石材成为可近距离观看的山岳想象。馆方将这类玉山联系到寻求仙境和长生的道教主题。玩家应区分历史信仰与科学事实，不能把古人认为玉可护身或延寿写成真实功效。图鉴关注如何在有限体量中组织山景，未有来源的宫廷使用场景与人物传说不作补充。中文名称与解释为待审订稿，具体信息可由原始机构链接复核。
本篇以1942.617号馆藏为依据。深绿色玉材上有镂空花纹与四个花式把手，开放的纹样让器壁的空隙也成为装饰。馆方把它放在清代城市消费和奢侈工艺扩展的背景下，而不只归给宫廷。玩家可从镂空结构理解雕刻难度与视觉效果。记录支持香具这一功能范围，但香料品种、制作作坊与原使用者没有确定信息，图鉴不会自行填入。中文名称与解释为待审订稿，具体信息可由原始机构链接复核。
本篇以1947.543号馆藏为依据。白玉扳指表面以浮雕表现龙与鼠，是把小型佩用器物变成装饰载体的例子。来源只明确形制、材质和图像，没有说明这件是否实际用于射箭。图鉴因而保留扳指名称，但不由名称直接推断使用经历。对玩家最有用的观察是圆环形主体与表面雕刻怎样相互配合，精确工艺步骤和象征意义仍留待专业审订。中文名称与解释为待审订稿，具体信息可由原始机构链接复核。
本篇以1952.480号馆藏为依据。这件马形玉雕被馆方放在文人案头物与收藏趣味的讨论中。小型器物既能供观赏，也能让书斋成为展示品味的场所；不过，本件具体是否用作镇纸并未因此得到确认。玩家可比较动物造型与材质处理，而不把所有案头玉雕自动分成实用文具。图鉴不添加马的品种、主人或皇家赠赐经历，只保留资料可支持的文化背景。中文名称与解释为待审订稿，具体信息可由原始机构链接复核。
本篇以1952.502号馆藏为依据。玉杯的交织龙纹以透雕形成，器物不仅在外壁刻图，也通过去除材料塑造通透结构。馆方强调它由圆形玉料加工，并联系到清代奢侈用品的需求。玩家可以注意纹样、器壁与空隙如何一起组织。杯的使用功能与工艺特点有来源依据，但是否为御用、是否曾供某位皇帝饮用没有证据，图鉴不作这种升级解释。中文名称与解释为待审订稿，具体信息可由原始机构链接复核。
本篇以1952.506号馆藏为依据。瓶体的截面为带弧边的菱形多面结构，兽面把手上悬着可以活动的环。活环与器身的关系让雕刻技术变得直观，也说明玉器可借鉴金属器的附件语言。馆方将其列入清代精工奢侈用品的背景。图鉴不把活环直接当作原始搬运功能的证据，实际使用、作坊和拥有者仍未知，玩家应先从可核对的形制认识它。中文名称与解释为待审订稿，具体信息可由原始机构链接复核。
本篇以1952.510号馆藏为依据。这件杯的断代曾从元代转为清代，馆方还以缺少乾隆款作为讨论是否到达宫廷的线索。它说明博物馆知识并非永久不变，新研究可能修订旧鉴定。图鉴只报告机构当前的归属，并明确缺款不能单独证明完整流传史。道教人物的具体身份、作者与作坊若没有充分说明，仍需审订，不借更新后的年代编造新的宫廷故事。中文名称与解释为待审订稿，具体信息可由原始机构链接复核。

圆盘形玉璧表面不是素面，而是以凸点和细刻旋纹组成斜向排列的谷纹。馆方将这种密集装饰与新石器时代较简单的璧形设计比较，展示一种长久延续的器形怎样改变表面表达。

玩家可以先看圆形和中央孔，再看纹样重复的节奏。“谷纹”是一种约定的装饰名称，不意味着器物用来储存粮食，也不能把每个小点都理解为真实种子的模型。它值得展示，在于有限面积能组织精密而一致的工艺。

本件来源年代为战国。它可为游戏汉代玉璧提供形制比较，却不能证明那个游戏定义的时代或身份。用途、出土地与拥有者若没有本件证据，仍保持待审。
本篇以1952.568号馆藏为依据。这件玉雕把道教仙人刘海蟾与蟾蜍组合起来，馆方将其置于财富象征的图像传统中。人物故事属于宗教与民间叙事，不是本件实际经历的考古证明。玩家可以关注人物、伴随动物与寓意之间的关系，同时保留对具体纹样的核验。图鉴不把传说生平当成可靠纪年，也不暗示玉雕具有现实招财能力。中文名称与解释为待审订稿，具体信息可由原始机构链接复核。

articles.body: 本篇以1952.573号馆藏为依据。小型玉雕把猫科面貌、牛角与象鼻组合在一起，形成并不存在于自然界的复合动物。馆方直接描述了这些组成部分，因此图鉴不必为它强行指定某一种神兽名称。它的知识点在于古代造型如何把熟悉的动物特征重新组织。用途、宗教含义与具体命名当前不足以确定，保留宽称谓比套用未经核验的专有译名更准确。中文名称与解释为待审订稿，具体信息可由原始机构链接复核。

articles.body:
坐姿人物带牛首与四角，肩部钻孔相互连通，使悬挂用途成为可以讨论的线索。馆方把它置于东北中国新石器传统，并以“可能”归入红山文化；这种限定必须与推荐中文名一起保留。

它的研究意义在于不同层次的证据。孔道是实物结构，悬挂是功能解释，巫者佩用则更进一步。玩家可看到一件物品怎样引出信仰讨论，却不必把每一种解释视为确定事实。展示时让这些层次并列，比给人物直接命名更可靠。

当前不能确认佩戴者身份或完整宗教用途。图鉴不把它写成已知某位巫师的护符，也不因动物头部混合形态而套用未经核验的神兽译名。

articles.body:

它能帮助玩家理解文字与实物断代之间的距离。款识是一条需要审查的材料，不是自动生效的制造证明；描写晋代诗人的作品，也不等于实物来自晋代。器形、书写与材料应一起讨论，才能避免把不同历史层混在一起。

推荐名称用“仿古”说明造型借用，不替专家解决年代争议。正文不复制诗文全文、不宣布确定作者，也不将陶潜说成这件玉器的持有者或制作者。

这只盘曾被作为高丽墓出土的白色青瓷介绍，馆方现在将它认作宋代中国青白器。它的特别之处，在于一件实物能同时留下海外发现背景和中国制造归属，而两者并不互相排斥。

浅淡釉色与刻花是认识器物的入口，鉴定修订则把阅读引向流通史。中国陶瓷可以被海外使用和收藏，因此发现地不是制造文明的快捷答案。玩家通过这一例子，能理解来源研究为什么必须分开工艺、产地与后来的埋藏地点。

图鉴报告机构当前归属，同时保留旧说的差别。不以“在某地出土”推定当地生产，也不补写具体运输者、墓主人或跨海贸易路线。

这件碗适合把观看从纹样引向制作。图案看似轻巧，却与胎、釉和烧造方法共同决定器物效果。玩家可以比较口沿与器腹的处理，理解技术痕迹也能帮助认识窑口，而非只依赖颜色或一个名贵称号。

articles.body: 本篇以1940.942号馆藏为依据。小型红釉瓶被馆方归为郎窑器，记录将其置于景德镇清代制瓷与奢侈消费的背景中。鲜明釉色是认识它的入口，但图鉴不会仅凭颜色把所有红釉都称作郎窑红。玩家应把釉色、形制和来源断代一起看。具体配方、烧造批次及原主人的身份并未给出，不能由工艺成就推演成一段宫廷使用故事。中文名称与解释为待审订稿，具体信息可由原始机构链接复核。

本篇以1942.127号馆藏为依据。这只茶碗有圆腹，褐黑釉上混有灰绿和棕色变化，釉层没有一直延伸到底足。馆方把它归为宋代福建建窑器。图鉴让玩家注意釉面与露胎处的关系，而不是给所有斑驳黑釉自动套上同一纹样名称。饮茶用途来自器物类型，具体茶法、主人与使用场所没有本件证据，仍留待相关研究核实。中文名称与解释为待审订稿，具体信息可由原始机构链接复核。

articles.body:
莲花从水波中伸出，凸起的轮廓把色彩分成多个区域。馆方描述的法华工艺是把泥料挤成线条，再将颜色填在其间烧成，使装饰既有图像也有触觉般的层次。

这件瓶的价值在工艺与题材互相配合。莲花在文人和佛教语境中都能获得意义，但细部并不只为讲故事：凸线帮助组织颜色，水波又引导观者沿瓶身观看。玩家可以把它与平面绘画式陶瓷装饰比较，理解器物表面并非一种固定画法。

来源关联景德镇制作，不等于本件必为寺院或某位文人所用。文化象征只能支持解释范围，具体委托者、使用地点和作者姓名仍需本件证据。

articles.body: 本篇以1969.32号馆藏为依据。盒子的龙、云和波浪以层层雕漆组织，长条外形服务于卷轴收纳。馆方将它联系到乾隆肖像卷的收藏与宫廷制作。图鉴概述这种关系，不复写长篇宫廷名单或把盒子当作肖像本身。玩家可比较储藏器与内装艺术品的不同身份。款识和档案解释仍需专业审核，不凭五爪龙就为所有类似漆器判定御用。中文名称与解释为待审订稿，具体信息可由原始机构链接复核。
本篇以1970.131号馆藏为依据。琥珀圆雕表现抱酒器而睡的李白，并搭配蝙蝠、鹿等图像。馆方把这些动物与吉祥寓意联系起来，形成文学人物与装饰趣味的组合。图鉴把造像题材与李白的真实生平分开，不将民间醉后捞月故事当作已证实死因。玩家应认识后世人物雕像也有其自身制作时代，而不是以所雕人物的年代给实物断代。中文名称与解释为待审订稿，具体信息可由原始机构链接复核。
本篇以1985.32号馆藏为依据。这件补子的媒材为缂丝，而不是笼统的绣片。馆方说明补子用于表达官阶，图鉴则强调织造方式与图像制度是两个不同层面。玩家能从中理解同一身份标志可由不同纺织技术实现。具体鸟兽种类与品级若未逐项核对，不作自动判定；服装制度的通用说明也不能替本件补出穿着者与流传史。中文名称与解释为待审订稿，具体信息可由原始机构链接复核。
本篇以1996.2.1号馆藏为依据。外层织物的联珠对鸭与内衬花纹来自不同丝绸传统，馆方将这种组合视为丝路文化交流的证据。关于为藏地王子制作、是否穿用或作为礼物，来源保留推测。图鉴同样保留这些限定，不把多地材料与流传背景压成单一产地。玩家可注意一件衣物内部也可能体现跨区域协作与交换。中文名称与解释为待审订稿，具体信息可由原始机构链接复核。

articles.body: 本篇以1929.981号馆藏为依据。白色石材上的躯干与姿势形成流动的曲线，馆方用肩胯的相反倾斜解释唐代雕塑的塑形特点。图鉴介绍的是可观察的姿态和宗教类型，不把残像补成某位已确认菩萨的完整形象。玩家可从缺失部分与保留线条理解残件仍有艺术价值。寺院、原供养人及破损原因未被确认，当前资料不支持虚构复原故事。中文名称与解释为待审订稿，具体信息可由原始机构链接复核。
本篇以1929.983号馆藏为依据。八角石柱残段的各面刻佛教图像和文字，馆方把它解释为信众为亡者供奉的经幢。宗教咒语被认为具有护佑作用，这是历史信仰的描述，不是现实效果。玩家应区分柱段与完整经幢，以及纪念文字与制作年代的关系。图鉴不抄写未经校读的碑文，更不会自行补上八个家庭的姓名或具体寺院。中文名称与解释为待审订稿，具体信息可由原始机构链接复核。

薄石灰岩片两面都有雕刻练习，不同头像的处理与完成度使它像一段留下痕迹的制作过程。馆方将其放在新王国时期，并对地点归属使用“可能”，因此不能把推测地点写成确定出土记录。

它值得展示，是因为博物馆不只保存完成的杰作，也保存工匠学习和试刻的材料。玩家可比较线条、头部轮廓与两面的水平差别，理解古代制作需要练习与选择。头像类型是机构的艺术史解释，并不等于画中人物都已识别姓名。

图鉴不编造课堂、工匠师徒关系或一次具体会面。练习片的用途有解释依据，但人物、作者及完整使用过程仍保持未定，来源原文可供逐项复核。

articles.body:
这块曲线形残片原属于拼嵌人物的头饰，浅蓝材料与较深的表层仍保留光泽。馆方认为整个人物可能为王后，但只是可能。费昂斯这一材料名称也不能简单等同中国瓷器或天然青金石。

它的研究价值在“残片如何说明组合”。轮廓和接口提示较大形象由不同材料拼成，颜色又参与表达人物的非日常身份。玩家可以从这一小件理解古埃及装饰如何将材料、色彩和宗教视觉联系起来，而不必补齐一张想象中的完整面孔。

原人物身份、建筑位置及其他嵌片都没有在本条得到确认。图鉴保留碎片状态和机构的限定语，不把一般颜色象征当成某位具体王后的证据。

细小石材被金质隔片分开，羽毛、身体和尾部因此各有清楚轮廓。馆方记录多种颜色材料，其中白色石料仍未识别。完整保留未知，比为了一张好看的材料表而猜出矿物名称更重要。

秃鹫头饰类型与女神、王后的图像有关，但本件并未由此对应某个已知人物。玩家可沿羽毛排列理解拼嵌技术怎样在小面积形成丰富细节，也能认识器物类型、人物身份和材料鉴定是三种不同问题。

来源支持图案与工艺的介绍，不支持补写佩戴者姓名、仪式日期或具体墓室。图鉴不会从金与宝石的组合直接推出王室所有权，仍需专业核验。

articles.body:
残件上保留一位站立者与一位坐者，高浮雕使姿态在石面上形成层次。馆方借更完整的墓碑比较原构图，并对人物身份与残存名字的复原提出可能解释，未将它们变成完整确定的铭文。

它适合讲述“告别图像”和研究方法。玩家可以从手势、容器和人物位置理解家庭纪念的表达，也应看到缺失部分怎样限制解释。展示残件并不一定比展示完整作品少知识，反而能让比较和复原的边界变得直观。

图鉴不会给亡者强定姓名，也不把其他墓碑的保存部分复制成这件的事实。原文中的“可能”和学者复原层次仍需保留，出土背景与人物生平继续待审。

它有吸引力的地方，是让玩家看到鉴定怎样工作。完整铆钉、少见纹样与金属材料都可能成为观察线索，但其中任何一项都不能脱离比较独立宣判。博物馆也会保存需要持续研究的对象，而不是只展示毫无疑问的答案。

图鉴保留争议，不写成确定的古希腊战场遗物。新研究年份属于知识更新，不是头盔制造年；游戏候选仍需另审，稀有度不能掩盖真实性的不确定。

articles.body: 本篇以1922.143号馆藏为依据。这幅雕版画描绘罗马广场上的古代骑像与后来的基座安排，作品自身却属于十六世纪。它展示古迹怎样通过旅行者购买的图像传播。图鉴把画中雕像、广场改建与纸上版画分成不同时间层。玩家不能因为主题古老就把版画列为罗马时代实物，作者与年份仍依机构记录而非画中人物的年代。中文名称与解释为待审订稿，具体信息可由原始机构链接复核。

articles.body: 本篇以1921.1701号馆藏为依据。面具有孔道等构造，馆方借同类物品讨论它可能被系在带服装与装饰的人形支架上。图鉴对本件陶材与比较中提到的石面具镶嵌严格区分，不能把其他材料的细节直接写到它身上。玩家可以理解“面具”未必就是实际戴在人脸上。功能与使用方式仍有推测，具体神祇或仪式身份不作编造。中文名称与解释为待审订稿，具体信息可由原始机构链接复核。
本篇以1921.568号馆藏为依据。披毯用毛与棉织成，带流苏，馆方介绍它在墨西哥独立后成为身份与自豪感象征的背景。这件属于十九世纪服装传统，而不是前哥伦布时期文明的器物。玩家可以认识世界藏品需要同时标明地域与时代。图鉴不因地域名称推定织作者，也不把一般文化意义变成这件曾由某位政治人物穿用的故事。中文名称与解释为待审订稿，具体信息可由原始机构链接复核。

articles.body: 本篇以1941.390号馆藏为依据。小型坐像持有的物件被馆方提出与水和新生植物相关的可能解释，但人物身份与用途仍神秘。材质名称依源记录保留，不自动译成某种确定玉石。玩家最值得理解的是研究也会诚实保留不知道的部分。图鉴不会把可能的海螺、植物或羽毛判定为已识别事实，更不会由坐姿编造祭司身份或具体仪式。中文名称与解释为待审订稿，具体信息可由原始机构链接复核。

石像虽失去头部，双手合拢的姿势仍让人注意到其奉献意味。馆方将它关联古地亚造像传统，并讨论类似像在神庙中代替统治者表达虔敬的作用。人物与宗教空间由此通过一件实物相连。

玩家可以理解肖像并不总是用于纪念或装饰，它也可能承担持续的礼敬表达。缺头没有使器物失去全部知识：姿态、材质与同类比较仍能提供线索。展示时，把保留部分和复原解释分开，比补出一副没有依据的脸更有价值。

图鉴不补写未校读的铭文、神庙名称或具体放置仪式。古地亚的历史背景与本件身份要分别核实，石像也不是人物遗骸或一段已证实事件的现场记录。

牛形小石雕的底面刻有奔跑动物，压在柔软材料上能留下图案；黑色嵌石则表现眼睛。一件物品因而有两个观看方向：立体的动物与平面的印面，而不只是简单的雕塑摆件。

它适合介绍实用与装饰的交汇。玩家可以从翻转器物的动作理解印面的工作方式，再观察形象如何承载身份或保护意味的可能解释。馆方给出的早期苏美尔文化标签与制作资料，为讨论提供依据，但印记内容仍不能直接当作文字姓名。

图鉴不推定它属于某位商人、某个行政机构，也不为其编造一份古代交易契约。具体用途和流传史需更完整证据；“护符”与“印章”的功能关系继续待专业审订。

articles.body: 本篇以1920.1975.a号馆藏为依据。这块另一馆藏号的石灰岩练习片保存多种头像，不能因题名和同类介绍相似就与其他习作合并。馆方讨论工匠如何练习不同人物类型，图鉴则把类型识别保留为机构解释。玩家可看到制作练习也能成为馆藏知识的来源。它并不支持一段具体课堂故事，工匠姓名、地点与完成过程未明确记录时继续未知。中文名称与解释为待审订稿，具体信息可由原始机构链接复核。

articles.body: 本篇以1920.1978号馆藏为依据。人物怀抱带神像的小龛，馆方将其联系到官员荷尔韦贾的宗教奉献与晚期埃及造像传统。这种构造让人物与神龛成为同一雕塑的两个观看重点。图鉴不把现代馆藏所在地当成古代奉献地，也不在缺少铭文校读时补写官衔全文。它可以说明政治身份和宗教表达如何相遇，但具体使用场景仍需来源逐项支持。中文名称与解释为待审订稿，具体信息可由原始机构链接复核。

articles.body: 本篇以1920.1979号馆藏为依据。石灰岩上的王者形象有意借用更早艺术的样式，馆方却将精细饰物等特点用于较晚时期的归属判断。玩家可理解“看起来很古老”不等于制造时代同样早。图鉴保留来源对仿古风格的说明，不由王像轮廓给人物指定姓名。断代依据需要专业比较，缺失的建筑背景和原始位置不会以一般埃及史代填。中文名称与解释为待审订稿，具体信息可由原始机构链接复核。

articles.body:
编号标本保存牙齿，馆方以Priconodon crassus登记，并给出早白垩世及地层信息。如此小的身体部位也能进入分类与地层研究，化石价值并不总依赖一具完整骨架或夸张的视觉体量。

展示时可以把三个层次分开：学名是机构鉴定标签，牙齿是保存部位，地质时期是形成背景。玩家由此理解一枚残件如何与更大的古生物知识网络相连，也能意识到当前文字并不等于我们已经重新完成专家鉴定。

推荐中文名保留属名，不强译未确认专业名称。采集日期晚于1933，不能让这件具体馆藏身份直接进入当年游戏世界；发现年、命名年与精确年龄继续保留未知。

来源名称仅为Genus sp，保存部位是不明肢骨碎片，地质资料指向始新世。这个宽泛名称体现当前鉴定程度，不应为了让图鉴更精彩就换成某一种恐龙或其他确定动物。

它值得展示，是因为科学馆藏不仅保存答案，也保存能继续研究的材料。骨片、地层与来源编号可以帮助后续比较，然而局部形态不能独立支持完整动物复原。玩家能在这里认识属、种和更高分类之间的差别，理解“不知道”也属于可靠知识。

图鉴保留机构原学名标签与待复核状态。采集时间不是化石形成日期，更不是自动得到的发现年；体型、生活环境与死亡原因没有本件证据就不补写。

本篇以PAL215308号馆藏为依据。标本保存部分右下颌及牙列，机构以Cupidinimus nebraskensis登记，并给出中新世相关地质标签。图鉴保留原学名和部位，不把一个局部颌骨扩大成完整动物骨架。玩家可以理解牙齿与骨骼片段在鉴定中为何重要，但具体分类结论仍需专家审核。出土地、采集者、地层与命名年份是不同信息，本件不会由其中一个日期自动补齐其他日期。中文名称与解释为待审订稿，具体信息可由原始机构链接复核。

articles.body: 本篇以PAL755132号馆藏为依据。原记录标题是研究项目名称，馆藏号却对应具体保管对象，来源给出新生代与地点信息，但未提供可靠的具体学名或保存部位。图鉴因此使用“未定名标本”的推荐名称，不把项目名当作物种。它适合说明数据库中的未知也应被保存。科学价值与运输方式还无法由这条记录充分判断，需要机构或专家补充后才能成为更具体的游戏提案。中文名称与解释为待审订稿，具体信息可由原始机构链接复核。

articles.body:
标本保存不完整椎骨，机构登记名为Clidastes affinis，地质标签指向晚白垩世。图鉴保留学名而不随意套用中文动物名，也不会把海生爬行动物题材笼统写成陆生恐龙。

这一残件的阅读重点在局部与整体之间。椎骨可以进入分类比较，却不足以让本稿确认整只动物的体长、姿态和生活行为。玩家可将保存部位、来源地点与地层信息并列观看，理解实物证据怎样支持研究，又怎样限制复原。

学名仍是来源给出的鉴定，尚非本项目专家复核结论。命名文字中的年份、采集时间和形成时代不能混用，缺失的实际发现年与精确年龄继续NULL。
本篇以PAL713207号馆藏为依据。机构把这件编号对象列在古植物类型及图示材料集合中，给出宾夕法尼亚亚纪相关地质标签，却未在本记录提供明确植物学名。图鉴不因类型集合名称就自动宣布它是某个物种的正模。玩家可以理解集合标签、类型地位和个体鉴定必须分别核对。保存形式与具体科学用途仍待补充，现阶段保留英文类别和待审订状态。中文名称与解释为待审订稿，具体信息可由原始机构链接复核。

articles.body:
机构记录给出Platycarya americana学名、始新世地质资料、正模标记与文献线索。这些信息让标本不只是一个自然图案，也与分类名称建立时使用的参照材料相联系。

玩家可以依阅读顺序认识实物、学名与文献：先看当前保存对象，再看机构对其科学角色的说明，最后沿资料链接理解研究背景。类型地位有源字段支持，但不意味着本项目已重新审核每一个鉴定结论，中文专业译名仍须审订。

采集年份、论文发表或命名时间、地质形成时代是不同信息。本文不补出未记录的精确年龄、叶形复原或气候结论，也不会把某个现代日期当作标本形成日期。

馆方以Sorbus carbonensis登记这件标本，并保存始新世、正模和文献信息。它为介绍古植物研究提供了一个真实编号的对象，而不是一幅想象中的史前森林插画。

收藏与展示的独到之处，是让观者理解分类依据可以被保管、复查和继续比较。玩家可把学名、类型标记与地层线索连起来看，却不能仅凭属名把本件保存形态复原得十分完整。对资料的克制，也是科学图鉴区别于奇观故事的地方。

目前中文专业名称与具体保存形态仍待核对。图鉴不添加未有证据的叶形、环境温度或生态结论，采集、发现和命名日期也不会相互代替。
本篇以V7号馆藏为依据。馆方记录保存下颌联合与一枚折断的獠牙，并以Mammut americanum登记，地质标签指向更新世。它不是完整骨架，图鉴也不把乳齿象属名直接当成猛犸象属。玩家可以从残件理解大型动物化石的保存与运输难题。具体体重、死亡原因及发现事件若未给出，继续未知，不能从一处断牙编出捕猎或灾难故事。中文名称与解释为待审订稿，具体信息可由原始机构链接复核。

articles.body:
来源以Beryl登记本件，并在变种、切磨与重量字段留下具体信息。它让玩家看到矿物分类和后期加工的区别：一个有学术名称的矿物，也可以成为经过切磨的宝石对象。

馆方的heliodor变种称谓不能自动变成“祖母绿”，所有绿柱石也不是同一颜色或宝石名称。展示时可比较原矿物身份与加工后的视觉效果，再讨论重量字段为什么只属于这件编号样本。未知成分和晶系不应用通用配方伪装为实测。

推荐中文名与译法仍待专业审订。产状、发现年份和原始晶体形态未充分记录时保持未知，现代切磨件的1933适配也需要独立策划审核。

馆方把蔷薇辉石列为主要矿物，并在同一记录注明方解石与黄铁矿等伴生矿物。这件样本的知识点在组合，而非只让观者记住一个漂亮的矿物名。

玩家可以理解一块标本并不等于一种纯物质。主矿物、伴生矿物和来源地点分别保留，能为材料比较与产状讨论提供入口，却不能从标题直接算出化学组成比例。展示时让不同层次的名称并列，比给全部表面统一贴上一个标签更准确。

具体矿脉、晶体尺寸与形成过程缺乏本件证据，因此不作推断。中文推荐名依据机构英文主矿物标签，仍待审订；源字段核对通过也不等于专家重新鉴定。

articles.body:
这件陨石小样保留正式编号、USNM馆藏号、重量和南极考察关联。分样很小，却能成为可反复研究的材料；它与整颗陨石不是同一个体量，也不能因编号相近便当作另一颗独立天体。

玩家可把身份、采集活动与科学观察分开。馆方的风化、裂隙说明属于样本资料，数字编号也需要规则解释，不能直接当作撞击年份。展示小样时，透明保留分样关系比编出壮观坠落现场更有知识价值。

本件的实际坠落或发现类型、陨石分类和精确发现年仍未确认。晚于1933的采集活动使具体馆藏身份需要时代阻断；未来游戏化原型必须另设身份，不能改写机构经历。
本篇以USNM 7629号馆藏为依据。来源保留陨石编号、微小重量与南极考察背景，还列有风化和裂隙等研究资料。图鉴不把分样序号当成第二颗独立陨石，也不根据测试缩写自行解释成未经确认的科学结论。玩家可认识真实馆藏的研究分样与整石之间的关系。记录年代比游戏世界晚，时代审查将阻止把本件具体发现经历直接移植到1933。中文名称与解释为待审订稿，具体信息可由原始机构链接复核。
本篇以NMNH 117343-21号馆藏为依据。馆方以Glassy basalt登记本件，并保存海洋考察、船只、采集时间与馆藏号等线索。图鉴把岩石名称与一次现代采样活动分开，不由船名推定新的地质形成日期。玩家可以了解岩石也有标本身份与研究履历。是否代表某种特定海底喷发、年龄与化学组成目前未充分给出，不能从“玻璃质”三个字编出精确成因。中文名称与解释为待审订稿，具体信息可由原始机构链接复核。
本篇以NMNH 117474-6号馆藏为依据。这件花岗岩记录有馆藏号、野外编号、实验室编号和采集者，说明自然史实物可以在不同研究环节有不同标识。图鉴将这些编号保留为追溯线索，不把它们合并成多个独立藏品。玩家可以理解岩石类型与个体来源各有价值。形成时代、具体矿物比例和开采经历未注明时保持未知，也不根据常见花岗岩知识为本件填入数值。中文名称与解释为待审订稿，具体信息可由原始机构链接复核。

records.description: Wine was often served hot in porcelain cups that could also be used in popular drinking games.

In the Qing dynasty (1644–1911), luxury items became more affordable to larger parts of the society, including women, merchants, and literati in non-official positions. Imperial patronage and a growing urban population encouraged consumption of luxury goods and local craftmanship. This enameled porcelain illustrates the the Qing dynasty accomplishments in porcelain techniques and the creative mind of the talented artisans who sought clients on a competitive market.
records.historical_period: China, Qing dynasty (1644-1911), Yongzheng mark and reign (1723-35)
records.original_name: Small Dish with Yellow Monochrome Glaze

records.description: The Water and Moon Guanyin is seated in the posture called "royal ease." His right leg is drawn up with folded knee; the left leg flexed. One hand rests on the upraised knee; the other extends downward to support weight on the palm. With gilding, the image assumes the splendor of divine dignity.

The bodhisattva is an enlightened being dedicated to the spiritual awakening of all beings. The compassionate bodhisattva Guanyin, in a variety of manifestations, is probably the most popular deity of worship in Chinese Buddhism. In the Esoteric Buddhist form shown here, this standing Guanyin has a total of eleven heads, with smaller ones above the principal head. The uppermost head represents the Buddha Amitabha, to whom he is closely related. The eleven heads symbolize the Buddha’s steps on the path to enlightenment.
records.historical_period: China, late Northern Song dynasty (960-1127) - Jin dynasty (1115-1234)

records.description: Seated on an intricate miniature stand, this polished nephrite (jade) egg features a cabochon ruby on top and a hinged gold-leaf border that reveals the interior. Within the egg, on a bed of gold, is a nest of even smaller eggs. Each red, white, and green egg mirrors an aspect of the larger egg, recalling the cleverness and meticulous details found within every House of Fabergé object.
This phoenix bird made of thin gold foil has tiny holes all along its edges, suggesting that it was sewn onto a textile.

These eight woodcuts (1959.99.8-15) progress from Gabriel’s announcement to Mary that she would bear the Son of God, to the events of her early motherhood and beyond. This included the joy of sharing her pregnancy with her cousin Elizabeth, Jesus’s birth, and the subsequent arrival of the magi. After Jesus’s circumcision and presentation at the temple the Holy Family fled to Egypt to avoid Herod and stayed there for several years. The seemingly out of place last scene shows a glimpse of their daily life in Egypt as Joseph continues his carpentry and Mary spins wool. The Holy Family is surrounded by angels and helpful putti and are blessed by God the Father and the Holy Spirit in the form of a dove overhead.

Printed books of hours were produced between 1485 and 1520. Significantly less expensive than handwritten production, printing made the popularity of books of hours soar. More than 1,775 different versions were printed during this time, allowing much customization. This hybrid version has printed text but hand-colored images and comes from Paris, a major center of book production.

records.description: Jewelry in ancient India often consisted of elements associated with water, such as fish and other aquatic plants and animals. Since water is essential for life, imagery that connotes water is life-affirming, or auspicious, and therefore appropriate adornment.

records.description:
Lan Ying’s painting is a gift to his friend, the Chan monk Wuyun, in which he depicted two sages of the Six Dynasties period: the Buddhist monk Zhidun (314–366 CE), and the Daoist priest Xu Xun (265–420 CE). Meant to be understood as an analogy of the friendship between artist and monk, the painting also offered a retreat into the past, a year before the fall of the Ming dynasty.

A professional painter born in Hangzhou, Lan Ying is traditionally considered a last representative of the Zhe school. Lan wrote poetic inscriptions and interacted with the literatus Chen Jiru (1558–1639).

There is a pomegranate design in each ogee (pointed arch) of this silk brocade fragment. The pomegranate is a small tree originating in Persia (today’s Iran) bearing fruit of deep red flesh filled with hundreds of seeds. The pomegranate has been revered as a symbol for health and fertility by many civilizations. In Islam the pomegranate is associated with paradise as described in the Qur’an.

This scroll depicts a spring scene with all kinds of birds, including one peacock with a hen among peonies. The painting is one of four surviving works by Yin Hong bearing his signature and seals. Some scholars debate whether this work depicts the theme “One Hundred Birds admiring the Phoenix,” a metaphor for human society presenting an idealized hierarchy under imperial rule; other scholars argue that peafowls, as exotic birds not native to China, would not be depicted to represent the emperor.

This large painting might have been hung in a palace hall and may have been part of a set depicting the four seasons.
records.original_name: Birds Gather under the Spring Willow

records.description: This masterfully composed landscape in light colors and delicate brushwork is an image of the water-rich Jiangnan region in southeast China, where Wu Bin was active as an artist. Embedded in rolling hills along lakesides and streams nestle cityscapes hosting numerous spring festivities. Lantern displays and street performances in the villages salute the New Year, and are interwoven with scenes of farming, fishing, and silk making. In one scene in the middle ground, an ox made of clay under a canopy is lead in a procession to an architectural compound, a ceremony known as whipping the spring ox in hope for a good harvest.

Spring peonies, summer orchids, and autumn chrysanthemums bloom at the same time amid garden rocks. These underglaze blue motifs were inspired by similar designs on Chinese ceramics made for export to Europe. In the early 1600s, Korean potters in Japan discovered kaolin, the clay essential for porcelain production. At the same time, political turmoil in China following the collapse of the Ming dynasty (1368–1644) disrupted Chinese exports. Together, these circumstances created an opportunity for Japan to supply ceramics to the European market. Careful study of Chinese prototypes shaped the work of Japanese ceramists for both domestic and overseas audiences.
records.original_name: Large Jar with Peonies, Orchids, and Chrysanthemums

records.description:
This painting represents bodhisattvas of the 10 stages of enlightenment undergoing the final processes toward Buddhahood. This and CMA 1973.70.2 form part of a set of scrolls that were used to perform the Water-Land (shuilu) ritual. The sinuous curves of scarf and drapery, the layering of garments, and the minute detail all reflect the opulent visual atmosphere that surrounded the Ming worshipper in temples and spirit halls throughout the country.

In the upper right corner of each painting is an imperial seal and an inscription in gold: Donated on the third day of the eighth month in the fifth year of the Jingtai reign (1454) of the Great Ming. Written in ink in the lower left corner is the record that they were made on imperial order, probably to present them to the Da Longfu monastery in Beijing.
records.original_name: The Bodhisattvas of the Ten Stages in Attaining the Most Perfect Knowledge

culture: 罗马与意大利历史文化
records.description: This bearded figure wears a tunic, trousers, and a soft conical hat with the apex bent over, called a Phrygian cap. He stands with his right hand raised (missing the index and little finger) and his left leg slightly bent. The figure originally held an implement in his lowered left hand, whose fingers curve around a shaft. The garments and cap identify him as a foreigner, likely a Dacian. Emperor Trajan (reigned AD 98–117) fought two military campaigns against Dacia (modern-day Romania), where he conquered and annexed the southern half of the region.

Within a roundel are a pair of mounted Amazons (women warriors) shooting backward at lions, which attack their running horses. The roundel frame is filled with stylized floral motifs and is bordered on the inside by a band of tiny hearts.
records.original_name: Roundel with Amazons, from a tunic

records.description: The decoration painted on this jar shows two multi-oared boats traveling through fertile riverbanks lined with trees and aloe bushes. Rows of triangles indicate the desert hills in the background. The Nile was Egypt’s primary means of transportation and communication, since river traffic was far more efficient than travel by land. The concept of boat travel permeated all aspects of Egyptian life and religion. The sun god Ra was believed to travel by boat across the heavens by day and through the underworld by night. Funerary texts describe the trip to the afterlife as a journey by boat, and scenes of boats figured prominently in tomb decoration.
Lobed Mirror with Two Phoenixes and Floral Displays, 8th century ad China, Tang dynasty (ad 618-907) CMA 1995.348 [Cat. no. 66.a]
records.original_name: Lobed Mirror with Paired Phoenixes and Floral Displays

records.description: The figure holding the skull has been identified as Mrgasirsa, who sought Buddha’s teaching on how to determine the karma and transmigration of the arhats. Mrgasirsa appears with Vasistha in some of the wall paintings of the Mogao grottoes in Dunhuang.

Bodhidharma is the legendary founder of Chan (Zen) Buddhism in China. Here he is seen meditating in front of a cliff, atop Mount Song. Behind him is his disciple Huike, the first recipient of his teaching.

records.description: Portable Buddhist figures and objects like this gilt bronze had a variety of uses. They could have been carried in religious processions. Others could serve as donations, souvenirs, or votive items in the context of pilgrimages to religious sites. Their miniature size also made them appropriate for placement on private altars or shrines for personal devotion.

Like the Teabowl with Tortoiseshell Glaze (CMA 2020.177), this jar was made in the Jizhou kilns of southeast China. Producing a variety of innovative dark glaze types, the potter here created a dynamic abstract pattern of waves in the form of light brown strokes brushed over a dark brown glaze.
records.historical_period: China, Jiangxi province, Jizhou kilns, Southern Song Dynasty (1127–1279) - Yuan Dynasty (1271–1368)

records.description: Jade is one of the hardest stones and requires an intensive, arduous process of abrasion—cutting, chiseling, grinding, and polishing—to achieve the desired shape. A grindstone and a slurry of grit and water shape the jade into the desired form, and then a cloth dampened and rubbed with finer grit may have been used to give the jade the smooth surface. For the Silla kingdom (57 BC–985), in particular, comma-shaped jades served as an essential item for the burials of the ruling class and were luxurious accessories to decorate golden crowns. Their comma shape is thought to represent embryonic forms, symbolizing life, particularly rebirth in the afterlife.
records.historical_period: Korea, Three Kingdoms period (57 BCE–668 CE)

locality.value: Balmaceda Raise, Antofagasta Prov, Chile, South America

records.description: Illustrated prayer books called books of hours remained popular with Europe’s elite well into the era of printing technology. This example belongs to a printed edition of five by the Parisian printer and engraver Guillaume Le Rouge, dating to 1510. Though printed on vellum (not paper), its 62 engraved pictures were hand-colored by an illuminator much like a traditional manuscript. By the mid-1480s, Paris was the center of production for books of hours with printed texts and engraved ornament. This book is therefore a hybrid fusing two distinct production methods—illumination and printing—representing the waning phase of the illuminator’s art prior to the complete transformation to printed books.
records.original_name: Printed Book of Hours (Use of Rome): fol. 66v, Text

records.description: The hair of this hollow, mold-made, female figurine was originally arranged in two projections atop the head. She carries an identical, small figure interpreted as a child; the figurine may be a metaphor for generational continuity.

records.description:
Poet Tao Yuanming (365–427 CE) turned down a career as an official in politically turbulent times to return to his home estate, northwest of Mount Lu, to write poetry and enjoy his garden and wine. Having an ailing foot, he was carried in a basket or walked with a staff. As he grew chrysanthemums, Tao is associated with this flower.

The artist Chen Hongshou, active in Zhejiang province, suffered through the violent transition from the Ming to the Qing dynasty around 1644. By portraying the poet who lived a millennium earlier during similarly fraught times, Chen intentionally chose an archaistic style.
records.original_name: Paintings after Ancient Masters: Portrait of Tao Yuanming

records.description: This jar still has its original cover, which is rare among surviving examples. Its missing knob most likely had the shape of a lotus bud. Beautifully carved lotus petals cover the vessel’s shoulder and lid under a translucent green glaze. In Buddhism, the lotus is a flower symbolizing purity and detachment from worldly affairs; its presence suggests that this vessel was meant to be used in a religious context. The well-crafted double loop handles may have held a silk cloth or other textile that would have been folded over the lid to keep it in place. This aesthetic prefigures the celebrated green celadons in adjacent regions.
records.original_name: Covered Jar with Carved Lotus Petals (lid)

records.description: Although quite schematic, the subject of this pendant is easily recognizable as a bird, likely a rooster. Cleverly designed to hang evenly from its central suspension loop, it comprises three main parts: long neck terminating in a head with a pointy beak and small crest; triangular body with stylized feet; and broadly arched tail feathers.
records.historical_period: Northern Greece, Macedonian, Geometric period  (900-700 BCE)

records.description: The Chupícuaro culture, located north of Mexico City in the state of Guanajuato, created a distinctive ceramic tradition including small clay figurines. This example is said to belong to a group of ten figurines from the same burial or cache (1990.145–154). The group includes both males and females that can be sorted into couples based on size.

Derived from his own pen-and-ink drawings, this suite of etchings features fictional characters situated near recognizable buildings and statues in Rome. On the title page, Robert dedicated the suite to Marguerite Le Compte, who visited Rome in 1764 in the company of the wealthy author and art enthusiast Claude Henri Watelet. Both Le Compte and Watelet were amateur etchers, and they socialized with a group that included artists and printmakers centered at the academies in Italy. Robert’s dedication was likely motivated by the hope of future patronage from Le Compte. She may be the generous woman with a hand muff depicted in The Ancient Temple, the fifth scene in this series.

This covered cylindrical jar with three animal feet is lavishly covered with a cobalt blue glaze in the exterior and an amber glaze in the interior.    Of the colored lead glazes of sancai (three-color) ware, blue was preeminent and precious. Imported cobalt from Persia (Iran, Afghanistan) was used as a glaze colorant that yields a rich, brilliant blue of considerable splendor.

The Willow and Magpie is the product of a mindset that combines knowledgeable observation of birds in general and magpies in particular with an image-making process using a sophisticated ink technique to suggest the nature of the bird, the general characteristics of willow, and the visual effect of rain and mist. These are not trivial accomplishments but of equal importance with Southern Song period achievements in lyrical poetry or canal building.

This nude figurine was likely inspired by the Aphrodite of Knidos by Praxiteles, a work that spawned countless reproductions of varying sizes in different media. Created from inexpensive terra cotta clay, this Aphrodite might have been commissioned as a votive offering by a person of modest means.

Both ancient Egyptian men and women loved cosmetics. Unguents, oils, and perfumes made from aromatic plant resins and gums were obtained at great cost from distant lands. The objects identified with cosmetics were given lavish treatment. The god Bes, patron god of cosmetics, is the subject of this colorful jar.
records.original_name: Cosmetic Jar in the Form of the God Bes

records.description: Like his colleague Claude Lorrain, Poussin depicted historical and mythological subjects in landscapes inspired by the countryside around Rome. His themes were often complex, and frequently incorporated witty allusions to classical texts. Here, a playful cupid tugs Pan, the goatlegged Greek god of the woods, toward Venus, the goddess of love. The painting cleverly illustrates the Latin phrase amor vincit omnia, or “love conquers all” (in Greek, pan means “all”). The woodland setting represents the idyllic paradise of Pan’s home.
records.original_name: Nymphs and a Satyr (Amor Vincit Omnia)

records.description: Pietro da Cortona drew this angelically beautiful face in a style reminiscent of the work of Renaissance master Raphael (1483–1520). Cortona's use of black chalk to develop extremely subtle effects of shading shows the technique at its most refined. He drew this sheet in preparation for a ceiling decoration, Saint Michael and Angels with the Instruments of the Passion, painted in fresco in the church of Santa Maria in Vallicella (better known as the Chiesa Nuova, or "New Church") in Rome, completed in 1633.
records.original_name: Study for the Head of St. Michael

records.description: The figure watching the stars is believed to be the messenger Zhang Qian (died 114 BCE). Legend says he lost his way in the Milky Way, where he met the Weaving Maid who gave him a stone from her loom. Zhang, in fact, holds a slab inscribed loom stone. The vessel is dated, inscribed, and has a seal of the silversmith Zhu Bishan, from Zhejiang province, who ran a workshop in the Lake Tai area near Suzhou. Zhu is one of the few Chinese silversmiths known by name, producing silverware so desirable that his name was used like a trademark by his competitors and followers. Made of pure silver, and shaped like a hollow log, the cup was assembled from several silver pieces that were then soldered together.
records.historical_period: China, Yuan (1271-1368) or early Ming dynasty (1368-1644)

records.description: Even though this statue of a king is uninscribed, its distinctive features identify it without any doubt as a portrait of Amenemhat III. The heavy brows, prominent cheekbones, hollow cheeks, jutting lower jaw, and tightly bunched muscles at the corners of the mouth make a strikingly realistic impression. Not realistic, however, are the king’s supersized ears. Instead, they symbolize the ruler’s willingness to hear the prayers of his people. If this image had been carved in relief, the king’s hands would have been uplifted in worship. Here, however, to prevent the breakage of projecting limbs, the ruler’s hands are pressed flat against the front his kilt, a portion of which is looped over his belt.
records.historical_period: Egypt, Middle Kingdom (2040–1648 BCE), Dynasty 12, reign of Amenemhat III (1860–1814 BCE)

records.description: In the Qing dynasty (1644–1911), imperial patronage and a growing urban population encouraged consumption of luxury goods and local craftmanship. Luxury items became more affordable to larger parts of the society, including women, merchants, and literati in nonofficial positions. This miniature porcelain vase with famille rose overglaze enamel decoration illustrates some of the highest technical accomplishments in Qing porcelain production.
records.historical_period: China, Jiangxi province, Jingdezhen kilns, Qing dynasty (1644-1911), Qianlong mark and reign (1736-95)

records.description: This teabowl exhibits a shiny almost mirror-black, thick glaze that runs down from the mouth showing fine, bluish-brown streaks around the rim. The Northern Song dynasty emperor Huizong (徽宗, reigned 1100–1126) once referred to the markings as “hare’s fur.” The emperor also remarked that Jian bowls should be deep and wide to allow tea powder to be whisked sufficiently in the bowl. The contrast between the tea’s white foam and the dark glaze was appreciated by connoisseurs. The thick walls and conical shape of the bowls were ideal for keeping tea hot and frothy.
records.historical_period: China, Fujian province, Southern Song dynasty (1127-1279)

records.description: In late Song dynasty Chinese Chan Buddhist temples, paintings of landscapes, animals, or plants frequently took the place of deities. This hanging scroll features the humble life of woodcutters in nature an is in keeping with the Chan emphasis on simplicity and on the spiritual benefits of manual labor. executed in broad, quickly applied washes and punctuated by dark dots and texture strokes, the work is inscribed by Xuzhou Pudu, a priest at Wanshou temple near the Southern Song capital at Lin'an (modern Hangzhou).

Concerned that his drawings did not do justice to the splendor of India’s monuments, Rousselet learned photography in India that year, a remarkable accomplishment. He proved to be a talented photographer with a sophisticated sense of composition. The scenes in this volume sweep across sites of Sultanate, Rajput, and Mughal power in northern India, from the sacred Hindu city of Varanasi on the Ganges River to Alwar in Rajasthan. Also included are several scenes of industry and portraits of Indian rulers.

His stooped posture suggests that he may have a physical disability, something rarely depicted in Greek art. His right foot and right hand (with bowl) are modern restorations done before the statuette came to Cleveland, perhaps in the 1800s.

records.description: An exercise for military troops, polo was also fashionable among men and women of Tang China, and this polo player is actually a woman dressed in a man's riding habit. It is in keeping with the exuberance of the Tang dynasty that such sporting figures of daily life should be among objects for the afterlife.

The butterfly often appears in the headdress of the Great Goddess, an extremely important Teotihuacán deity. This bowl was potted using the marbling technique called jiaotai (mixed clay), whereby light- and dark-colored clays are combined to create natural patterns, then covered with a transparent glaze. The marbling technique had been developed since the 8th century in imitation of the marbled glassware imported from Persia. Song marbled ware represented the continuation of the Tang tradition, achieving simplicity and vibrancy in aesthetic effects.

His posture and expression are tense and serious, reflecting the sobriety of this period in Egyptian art.

Two lively dragons, with eyes and mouth wide open and tongue straight out, are accompanied by two felines to form the arched handles.

records.description: In the process of mummification, the liver, lungs, stomach, and intestines were removed, separately embalmed, and stored in specialized jars known as canopic jars (after a sailor in Greek mythology, who died at the town of Canopus in the Nile Delta and was worshipped there in the form of a human-headed jar). Each organ was identified with one of four funerary deities collectively known as the Sons of Horus: the liver with Imsety (man's head), the lungs with Hapy (baboon's head), the stomach with Duamutef (jackal's head), and the intestines with Qebehsenuef (falcon's head). It was their duty to protect the deceased and restore to him his body parts in the hereafter.

records.description: While dark-glazed ceramics resemble black lacquer ware, and celadons were often compared to green jade, white or bluish-white glazed stoneware imitates silver. Here, broad silver bands around the bowls’ rims accentuate their precious appearance. The incised petals are inspired by lotus flowers and the domed covers by their circular leaves. The lotus motif often indicates the use of an object in a Buddhist context, in which it is a symbol of purity as its flowers emerge unsullied from the mud of lakes and ponds. Alternatively, these bowls may have been used to hold food at banquets.

records.description: This intaglio, or engraved gem, depicts an eagle with wings partially spread, a lightning bolt clutched in its feet. The bird looks to the upper right, suggesting it may be about to take flight. This gem is expertly carved, with each individual feather of the eagle described with thin lines. The eagle was a symbol associated with the Roman imperial family, Roman military, and Jupiter, the supreme Roman deity. The setting is likely ancient, and it retains traces of enameling in some loops.

records.description: In 486 BC, Xerxes succeeded Darius I as king of Persia. His empire, then the world’s largest and most powerful, encompassed an area from Libya to western India and from Ethiopia to Afghanistan. This relief fragment of one of his guards probably comes from the west stairway of his enormous palace at Persepolis. As chronicled by Herodotus, the Greeks defeated Xerxes in a clash of conflicting political systems: democracy and monarchy.

records.description: This relief is one of four produced for the ciborium (canopy) erected by Cardinal Guillaume d'Estouteville over the high altar of the church of Santa Maria Maggiore in Rome. The ciborium was taken apart in 1747 and the other three panels--Christ Blessing, The Annunciation, and Saints Peter and Paul--were set into the walls of the sacristy.

This richly ornamented stone construction is the long, front side of a coffin platform ultimately derived from raised wooden beds that are still popular in China today. Now in five pieces (presumably cut to facilitate transportation after it was excavated in the 1900s), the three legs and horizontal spans may have originally been created as a single massive slab. Sockets cut in the top of the stone (some of which overlap the modern divisions) show how this slab would have been linked to the back with crosspieces also capable of supporting a top surface of flat stone planks.

Like the few examples discovered intact in northern Chinese aristocratic tombs, the most elaborate decoration occurs on the front surface of the coffin platform. The design is dominated by the three large vertical panels, corresponding to the legs, that contain animated high-relief depictions of three directional guardians: the White Tiger of the West, the Red Bird of the South, and the Green Dragon of the East. These three, along with the Snake-Entwined Tortoise of the North and the Yellow Dragon of the Center, were mainstays of Chinese cosmology linked, in a system devised as early as the Han dynasty, to elements (wood, fire, earth, metal, and water), functions, planets, and musical tones, among others. Not only illustrating the persistent appeal of these traditional apotropaic symbols, this scheme suggests that the platform was placed against the back, northern wall of a tomb that would have been entered from the south. The layered carving technique of these principal motifs as well as the shallow relief dragons, masks, and tendrils engraved in the horizontal spans recall forms found in both imperially sponsored tombs and cave chapels of the late sixth century.

This gold coin represents the reign of the Kushana ruler, Havishka. The coin bears a portrait of the ruler on the obverse and various deities on the reverse. It is identified by inscriptions in Kharosthi, the language used in northwestern India during the Kushan period.

This precious lacquer box is decorated with bird and plant motifs and figures in mother-of-pearl inlay. The decoration depicts the leisurely pursuit of scholars in nature and a garden setting. Scholars play the board game weiqi, have philosophical conversations, pluck a qin (a zither-like instrument with strings), and read books.

Lacquer chests of this type were used to store garments neatly folded along their straight seams. The mother-of-pearl inlay from shells is a technique that was typically practiced by craftsmen in Hangzhou and other parts of southeast China near the sea.

German Romantic artist Ernst Fries was known for experimenting with various printmaking techniques, including etching and lithography. Fries lived in Rome from 1824 through 1827 and made this print during his time there. A collaboration with Munich architect Joseph Thürmer, the work offers a panoramic view of the city from the tower of the Capitol and highlights recent excavations. In his travel memoir, Italian Journey, Johann Wolfgang von Goethe advised that visitors to Rome study Fries and Thürmer’s print to evoke an evening he himself spent in the area depicted as the sun set, and to “imagine for themselves the blazing colors with their shadowy blue contrasts and all the magic which the scene derived from them.”
records.original_name: View Towards Rome from the Capitol

records.description: During the long, peaceful reign of Amenhotep III, Egypt reached a pinnacle of wealth and splendor. This magnificent portrait captures the ruler's exotic features to perfection. He has large, almond-shaped eyes, elegant arched eyebrows, and a full mouth. His face is youthful and without blemish. The bone structure is lost in the fleshy fullness of the face. The contrast between polished and roughened surfaces is a hallmark of hard stone images of Amenhotep III. The flesh areas were smoothed to a glistening sheen, while the eyeballs and the crown were left rougher. The roughening of the crown also had a practical purpose, for the upper portion was originally painted blue and the browband was painted yellow. The paint would have adhered better to the unpolished surface.
records.historical_period: Egypt, New Kingdom (1540–1069 BCE), Dynasty 18, reign of Amenhotep III (1390–1352 BCE)

The flared mouth, toothless gums, and fangs are typical of Olmec supernatural beings. The meaning of the body's "four-dots-and-a-bar" motif is unclear, but it sometimes appears in depictions of plants. The deity, then, seems to be associated with fertility.

records.description:
Poem and painting, once mounted together as one fan, exemplify the collaboration between imperial patron and court painter. Emperor Lizong’s calligraphy cites a verse from Wang Wei’s (701–761) poem, Walking to where the water ends, I sit and watch when clouds arise.

Ma Lin’s response is this painting. At the water’s edge, a scholar reclines by a large rock. The view leads across the empty middle ground to a distant mountain. With sparse ink and subtly graded washes, Ma Lin visualizes the poetic verse. The painting suggests the impact of Chan aesthetics through interaction between the palace, literati-officials, and monasteries around Hangzhou.
records.original_name: Scholar Reclining and Watching Rising Clouds, Poem by Wang Wei

records.description: This grave marker takes the form of a lekythos, a type of vase (usually ceramic) commonly left as a grave offering in ancient Athens. Now fragmentary, it once had a foot below and a thin neck and vertical handle above. Five sculpted figures adorn its front. At left, an unnamed woman holds an infant. To their right, a woman, Lysistrate, clasps hands with a bearded man, Timophon. Between them stands a young girl, likely Kleippe, although her name is partially lost. The scene may commemorate Lysistrate’s death in childbirth, mourned by her husband and older child. Her newborn child apparently survived.
records.original_name: Gravestone in the Form of a Lekythos

records.description:
In this hanging scroll birds rest and frolic among pines, bamboo, and flowering plum, plants known as “the three friends.” Due to their endurance in winter, they symbolize perseverance and friendship in adverse times. The naturalistic depiction of the birds refers to the bird-and-flower painting tradition of the Art Academy of the Song dynasty.

The painter Bian Wenjin served at the court of the Ming dynasty Yongle Emperor (reigned 1402–24). This painting may have been hung in a private studio or palace hall on appropriate occasions.
records.original_name: A Hundred Birds and the Three Friends

records.description:
Jiao Bingzhen, a court painter largely active during the reign of the Kangxi Emperor, was the senior artist on this fan. Jiao painted the Manchu horse trainer and the setting into which the horse was inserted by Giuseppe Castiglione. Each artist was bonded to his own artistic tradition, while flexibly and harmoniously accommodating the others’ style.

Jiao’s brushwork displays rigor and control, particularly in the twisting and turning trunk of the willow. The treatment of the figure and his clothes is an exercise in linearity. The horse trainer’s gesture and posture closely adhere to the known repertoire of the Chinese figural tradition, but the specificity supplies a sense of documentary reportage of life on the frontier. His shaved forehead and white temples identify him as a Manchu. The thick fabric of his garments was defined in a different sort of brush line than Jiao typically used for Chinese scholars or travelers.

Jesuit priest Castiglione, a newcomer to China at the time this was painted, brought a sense of Western realism to the horse. Poised at a slight angle, the horse is alert, its eye gleaming. Its contours suggest the bulk of its anatomy with skilled but not overpowering modelling, and careful and subtly wrought attention to detail, such as fluttering strand of mane.

Because of his ability to combine traditional Chinese painting techniques with Western methods of perspective and chiaroscuro, Castiglione went on to be the most favored and honored of the missionary artists who served the early Qing emperors. Throughout his career, in addition to imperial demands for portraits and records of court events, Castiglione continued to paint favored imperial horses. These animal subjects reflect the desire of Kangxi and his successors to celebrate their nomadic origins and to keep alive the martial prowess of the Manchu warriors in their new and sedentary world of conquered China.
records.original_name: A Vignette of Life on the Frontier

records.description: Chinese mirror-casting achieved new elegance and precision with the technical development of stamped clay molds over which molten bronze was poured. A small rectangular unit of design was repeatedly stamped to create this background of curls and granulation, which resembles feather-covered textiles known from early tomb finds. The dominant pattern of slanting "T," pressed down upon the mold after the overall background stamps, corresponds to the modern Chinese character for shan (山 or mountain). Whether the pattern was symbolic or decorative during the Zhou Dynasty is unknown. The site of manufacture is probably south China, since many mirrors of this type have been excavated from tombs in that area.
records.historical_period: China, probably State of Chu, possibly Hunan province, Eastern Zhou dynasty (770–256 BCE), Warring States period (475–221 BCE)

records.description: Many sancai or "three-color" lead-glazed wares-such as this ewerare notable for their heavy dependence on metalwork prototypes. Such polychrome glazed wares were intended for the tomb.

This boxer raises his arms to pull tight the thongs (now lost) that Greek and Roman boxers wound around their hands for protection. The sinuous body curve and long proportions are characteristic of the late Hellenistic period, when artists created more elongated versions of athletes and other classical figures.
records.historical_period: Greece, Greco-Roman Period, late Ptolemaic Dynasty

records.description: The ruyi scepter was among the decorative items collected by the Chinese literati. It was thought that lofty and refined men of ancient times—the Seven Sages of the Bamboo Grove of the late 200s CE—carried ruyi scepters during the so-called pure conversations of the Daoists. The name ruyi (literally, as one wishes) conveys blessings of wish fulfillment. The fungus-shaped head is an emblem of immortality.
records.original_name: Scepter in the Shape of a Ruyi Fungus

records.description: Formerly ascribed to the French painter Simon Vouet (1590-1649), Rest on the Flight into Egypt has only recently been attributed to Poerson, a collaborator and follower of Vouet. Intended to be a small devotional picture, this painting on oak panel depicts a quiet scene of the Holy Family resting; the Virgin Mary sits while an angel brings the plump young Christ Child fruit, and St. Joseph leads their donkey away to graze. The delicate pinks and blues and the transparent treatment of light and shadow create a gentle domestic atmosphere, characteristic of Vouet's Italian-influenced work.
records.original_name: Rest on the Flight into Egypt

records.description: Both ancient Egyptian men and women loved cosmetics. Unguents, oils, and perfumes made from aromatic plant resins and gums were obtained at great cost from distant lands. The objects identified with cosmetics were given lavish treatment.
records.historical_period: Egypt, Greco-Roman period (332 BCE–395 CE), Ptolemaic dynasty (305–30 BCE)

records.description: The p'ing-t'o technique of inlaying gold and silver foil on lacquer produced luxurious articles of elegance and fragility. These stray silver inlays were originally mounted on a mirror back or a cosmetic box whose lacquered surface has disintegrated. They combine auspicious symbols of Indian and Chinese origin: human-headed birds whose melodies filled the Buddhist paradise, and bird-riding deities who inhabited the skies of Taoist mythology. Like these imaginary beings, the lions were probably paired in a radial design; at least one has been lost.
records.original_name: Inlays for a Mirror or Box

records.description: Even without his club or lion skin, the short curly hair and full curly beard identify this miniature head as that of Herakles. The eyes and mouth were likely once inlaid. His upward gaze suggests the head may be based on the Herakles Epitrapezios by Lysippos, the personal sculptor of Alexander the Great. The original Herakles Epitrapezios survives only through copies, including this one as well as a slightly later marble version also in Cleveland (among many others). This head was refashioned into a weight, probably in the Roman period, by filling it with lead and adding holes for a hook.
records.original_name: Head of Herakles Refashioned as a Weight

records.description: This early view of the entrance to the ancient Karlie, or Karla, Caves in Western India shows the site before its restoration, including the monumental entrance pillar topped by a sculpture. Windows cut into the rock provided light inside. The shrines, created between the 2nd century BCE and the 5th century CE, provided sanctuary and shelter for monks but also for travelers and traders.
records.original_name: Caves of Karlie: No. 1, The Approach

records.description: Like the firearms themselves, powder horns were made as courtly accessories to be worn as objects of beauty. Most Mughal nobles also served as military commanders, and accouterments of war would be worn as part of their formal attire. For this reason, artisans used precious materials such as white jade, which in this example has been carved with leaf and petal patterns, its natural black inclusions treated as ornament. Pressing down on the simple mechanism opens the hollow inner chamber from which small amounts of gunpowder were administered into the pan of a matchlock musket.

This statuette of Isis and Horus is a better than average example of an extremely common type. Isis offers her breast to her son Horus, who is seated on her lap. With her left hand she cradles the young god, while with her right she clasps her left breast. She wears a striated divine wig, vulture headdress, and uraeus, the details of which are finely incised. Above her are the modius, cow's horns, and a sun disk.
Horus sits at a right angle to his mother, his arms at his side. He wears the sidelock of youth and a uraeus. He is nude except for a broad collar and a chain from which is suspended a heart amulet.
records.historical_period: Egypt, Late period (715–332 BCE), Dynasty 26 or later

records.description: Delicacy and refinement, combined with simplicity of shape, make Ding ware particularly attractive. The best pieces were selected by the Northern Song court for imperial use. The white, thin body is covered with a transparent ivory glaze that occasionally runs down toward the foot, forming streaks or drops called "tear-stains" by the Chinese connoisseurs. As the vessel was fired upside down, the rim was unglazed and could be bound with a metal band, such as copper or precious silver and gold.
records.historical_period: China, Hebei province, Quyang, Northern Song dynasty (960-1127)

records.description:
By the 1500s, visits to historic and scenic sites in the lower Yangzi delta stimulated an increase of printed illustrated travel books. Topographical depictions of local scenery flourished.

Leaves from this album illustrates sites around Lake Tai of the two adjacent counties Changxing and Wuxing (modern Huzhou). Song Xu, who lived intermittently in Jiaxing and Songjiang, must have passed through Wuxing by boat and thus knew the region.

The paintings are inscribed with gazetteerlike notations, suggesting that the album was produced for clients as commemorative works, a travel guide, or for “armchair travel” (woyou) in one’s mind.

culture: Pakistan, Gandhara, probably Sirkap, early Kushan period
records.description: Tiny reliquaries holding the cremated remains of the Buddha or a high-ranking holy person empowered monuments and made them sacred. A Buddhist monument, such as the solid hemispherical mounds called stupas, would not be worshipped until it was consecrated with the relic secreted inside. Bits of ash were combined with tiny gems inside a crystal or glass reliquary, which was then placed inside a stone or metal container, like the lidded versions seen here. These containers look like cosmetic vessels for aromatic pastes used for perfume in ancient India. Buddhist texts state that the enlightened Buddha emitted a fragrance like sandalwood paste; the form of the reliquary as a perfume bottle indicates the presence of the Buddha by the visual reference to his pleasant scent. Once enclosed in the stupa the reliquaries would not be seen, but monks were tasked with applying sandalwood paste to the exterior of stupas as part of their regular maintenance to convey to visitors the ongoing presence of the Buddha radiating from the relic in the center.
records.historical_period: Pakistan, Gandhara, probably Sirkap, early Kushan period
records.original_name: Miniature Stone Reliquary or Toilette Casket

records.description: The silver inset of this mirror back was decorated with several hand-beaten techniques. High-relief birds, beasts, and foliage were hammered from the underside (repoussé) and finely chiseled on the front (chased). The background and border were punched with a metal stamp of tiny circles. Mirrors of this precious material, diminutive size, and starlike form number among the most refined products of Tang metalworkers. Some historians suggest that miniature mirrors were specifically designed as burial gifts for children, but Tang gold and silver cosmetic boxes of similar scale indicate that these objects were made to grace the dressing tables of elegant women.

Carved in high relief, the original composition of this Attic grave marker can be reconstructed by comparison with more complete examples elsewhere (such as the Stele of Hegeso in Athens [National Archaeological Museum, 3624]). The standing figure at left likely represents a maid or servant, her hair mostly contained within a sakkos (haircloth). Holding a pyxis (small container) in her left hand, she approaches the more fragmentary seated figure at right. This woman, draped and casting her eyes downward, represents the deceased, perhaps Phanostrate, as one scholar has restored the partial name Phan... inscribed in the fragmentary epigram on the preserved portion of the lintel.

records.description:
This album of landscape paintings depicts the famous scenic areas located in and around the city of Wuxing in southeastern China. These places were all known for their natural beauty, but in addition, a number were distinguished by their links to eminent historical figures and events. The artist, Song Xu, was not a native of Wuxing, but must have visited it when he accepted the commission, for he carefully depicted all eighteen views and wrote comments on each of them.

Song's gazetteer-like notation on this leaf reads:
Baoyang Lake: Several li (Chinese mile) from here to the east, one can exit through Lake Tai, which is quite near. Just a few li to the north is the township of Xiangshan. Having arrived there, one may want to cross over the border to the city of Yixing.

The earliest Teotihuacan figurines are hand modeled, while later specimens were produced with molds. This exceptionally large example has a mold-made head, with facial features carefully retouched by hand. Earthenware figurines were made in great abundance throughout Teotihuacan's history, and may have been used in household religious rituals.

records.description:
The twenty paintings in this double album by Chen Hongshou include landscapes, figures, and flowers. It also has one leaf featuring a woman, an often-used subject not found in the other albums from the latter part of his career. His late works are wonderful summations of Chen's peculiar and quirky art—archaistic, hyper-refined—but without accompanying shallowness or sentimentality.

His figures and landscapes in the late albums are miniaturized, not unlike the small Chinese gardens, or the carefully selected small table rocks or old roots used for contemplation to see the world in miniature. This loss of scale is quite deliberate and reflects the psychological situation of a depressed class like the Ming loyalist officials and scholars, deprived of their integrity and honor, and forced to lead a diminished and restricted existence.

This spectacular vase, one of a pair in the collection, depicts flowering and fruiting peach trees to convey an auspicious message of affluence and long life. Developments in enamel technology led to new possibilities in polychrome decoration of Qing imperial porcelains. Pinks appeared, lending their name to the new palette of overglaze colors (famille rose), and the addition of opaque white allowed painters to vary the value of pigments, enhancing the painterly quality of porcelain decoration.

records.description: This white jade is carved as a double peach with realistically detailed leaves and branch following the curve of the jade. Clinging to the edge are a pair of bats, which represent good fortune.

Precious Sassanian and Central Asian metalwork had been imported to China as early as the 4th and 5th centuries as a result of wars and prosperous trade along the Silk Road. With the influx of foreign metalworkers to cosmopolitan Tang China, the techniques of sheet metalworking were introduced to the Chinese. This silver vessel demonstrates the effects of such east-west exchanges along the Silk Road. Its decoration with intricate gilt, incised and chased designs against a ring-punched ground is of a particularly high standard.

records.description: The tragic figure Orestes appears three times on the front of this sarcophagus, always wielding a short sword. In the center he stands over the body of his mother Clytemnestra, and at center left over the body of her lover Aegisthus. Orestes has killed them both to avenge their murder of his father Agamemnon, upon his return from years of fighting at Troy. At the far left, three Furies (avenging spirits) rest upon Agamemnon's tomb, while at the far right, Orestes atones for the murders at the Delphian shrine of Apollo, marked by a tripod and rock. On the lid, four reclining women symbolize the seasons, arranged in right-to-left order: Winter, Spring, Summer, Autumn, as indicated by their dress and the contents of their baskets.
This pair of cong-shaped vases was inspired by Neolithic jades of the Liangzhu culture. They reflect the Song scholar’s interest in antiquity and archaeology.
records.original_name: Pair of Vases in Shape of Cong: Southern Celadon Ware

records.description: Instead of depicting a real landscape, the artist focused on the rhythmic forces of nature and the movement of energy, using the scrolling form as a symbol common to all changes in nature: cloud vapors, waves, and mountains alike. Here a dragon hovers among sweeping scrolls.

This magnificent gilded bronze vessel with openwork decoration shows all kinds of fabulous creatures, real and imaginary, chasing each other among swirling scrolls. There is an emphasis on the unbroken rhythms of movement, rather than the ferocity of animals in combat. Cylindrical bronze vessels in this shape, called lian, were often used as cosmetic boxes.

records.description: In Greek art, the kriophoros is usually a shepherd or, later, Hermes. This statuette may be unique in presenting a warrior-hero as kriophoros. It is certainly one of the earliest sculptural representations of this type. The figure appears to be wearing a helmet, secured under the chin with a painted strap. Double outlines, reinforced at the bottom with incision and adorned with dotted circles in the area of the nipples, were used to suggest breastplates. A thick waist belt, decorated with painted crosshatched lines, is clearly the heroic zoster (warrior's belt). As described in ancient Homeric poetry, the zoster is the ultimate symbol of valor and prowess, worn by such heroes as the brothers Agamemnon and Menelaos and old King Nestor. This figure is shown in the solemn act of presenting a ram, most likely as a sacrificial offering, to a god or goddess.

records.description: These rare, elegant bronze bells were made in a tribal village along the southern borders of China. They differ greatly from bells made in the central regions, which often come in large sets and in varying sizes, and feature complex decorative patterns. The distinctive shape of these bells resembles a tall helmet topped by a pair of horns. A rope may have been tied around the horns so that the bells could be suspended. Each bell is decorated with a diamond-shaped insignia—probably to mark tribal affiliation. Although the bells are identical in size, each produces a different tone, which indicates that their casting was a highly refined process.
records.original_name: Set of Bells with Diamond-Shaped Insignia

records.description: Jewelry in ancient India often consisted of elements associated with water, such as fish and other aquatic plants and animals. Since water is essential for life, imagery that connotes water is life-affirming, or auspicious, and therefore appropriate adornment.
records.original_name: Necklace Bead in the Form of a Fish
Mirror with Serpentine Interlaces and Angular Meanders

records.description: Four or six squares of this luxurious two-color silk were originally sewn on a linen tunic, two positioned above the hemline in the front and two in the back, and possibly two more at the shoulder. The folded edges are still visible, including a silk sewing thread on the right side. The brittle condition is evident in the numerous crisp breaks.
records.original_name: Roundel from a Tunic with Palmette Tree

records.description:
In history, China moved from an original floor culture to high chairs and tables, developing a unique tradition of craftsmanship. Although still relatively unexplored, the manufacturing and styles of furniture differ by region.

This horseshoe-back armchair was made in Jiangsu province. Its simplicity and minimalist elegance is characteristic of Suzhou-style furniture and aesthetics. The back of the chair is made of seven pieces of wood, joined and secured with an inserted wooden pin, a mortise-tenon technique that appeared in its earliest form in Neolithic fragments of the Hemudu culture.
records.historical_period: China, Jiangsu province, Ming dynasty (1368–1644) or Qing dynasty (1644–1911)

records.description: Amorous couples were among the most prevalent imagery on the exterior of sacred sites in early India. Their life-affirming imagery was considered auspicious. This roundel would have been part of a brick structure, since terracotta was typically used in the ornamentation of brick temples, instead of stone.
records.historical_period: Northern India, Uttar Pradesh, Ahichchatra, Gupta period (c. 320-550)

records.description: The base of this statue is inscribed with the name and title of the supervisor of palace attendants, Minnefer. He is represented as young and athletic, hands at his sides and left foot forward, the typical striding pose for male figures. To make the statue more lifelike, the flesh areas were originally painted reddish brown, the wig black, and the kilt white. This was one of four statues of Minnefer that were found in the serdab (sealed statue chamber) of his ruined mastaba (tomb) in the cemetery west of the Great Pyramid at Giza. Most Old Kingdom private statues were concealed in this way. The statue was regarded as more than just a representation. Once the proper rites had been performed, it functioned as a substitute for the deceased individual and could partake of food offerings necessary for the survival of his ka, or vital spirit.
records.historical_period: Egypt, Giza, Old Kingdom (2647–2124 BCE), Dynasty 5

records.description: Pyxides came in a huge variety of sizes, shapes, and materials in the ancient world. Images of pyxides in Greek art often show them being used by women, which has led scholars to believe that they may have been used to hold jewelry or cosmetics. This pyxis is one of few surviving examples made from stone, signifying that it may have had an elite owner.

Sizable jade boulders of mountainous landscapes were carved to represent the search for the paradise or immortals' dwellings in the mountains. This Daoist theme has fired the Chinese imagination throughout history. Believed to have spiritual and magical properties, jade has long been used in tombs and intended for preserving the corporeal body and the soul in the quest for eternity. It is recorded that Daoist practitioners drank morning dews with scraps of jade as an elixir of immortality.

Giovanni Francesco Barbieri (called il Guercino) created Rest on the Flight to Egypt as a tondo, a circular canvas rarely used in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries except in the case of holy subjects. The round shape represents the circle, symbolic for the nature of God, believed to have no end and no beginning. The painting depicts Mary the Mother of God, the Infant Christ, St. Joseph, and a musical angel, serenading the Holy Family during their exhausting journey through Egypt. Guercino, "the squint-eyed", was born near Bologna and became an influential painter in Rome in the early seventeenth century, where he created important commissions. His style was an important mix of the strong use of tenebrism, introduced by Caravaggio, and artists of the classical baroque, such as Domenichino, Annibale Carracci, and Guido Reni. The composition is clearly composed with strongly modeled forms and a cool harmony of colors. The sleeping Infant Christ is lulled to sleep by the angel's violin and the ideal landscape with classical ruins adds to the calm serenity of this painting.
records.original_name: Rest on the Flight into Egypt

The sarape (wearing blanket) is a classic Mexican men’s garment that became a symbol of national identity and pride after Mexico achieved independence from Spain in 1821. Examples woven between about 1750 and 1875 in Saltillo, a town in northern Mexico, are the sarape’s most famous representatives, prized for their design, color, and technical refinement.

This early form of the Buddha image depicts him seated on an altar under the Bodhi tree. A coiled topknot of hair and elongated earlobes refer to his life as a prince when he wore a turban and heavy earrings. Behind his head is a solar disk, like a halo, and lions on the throne indicate the spreading of his teachings in all four directions.
records.historical_period: Northern India, Uttar Pradesh, Mathura, Kushan period

records.description:
This mirror bears an important inscription as well as symbolic imagery of the Eight Trigrams and Heaven and Earth to express the ancient Chinese cosmological ideas. The inscription reads:
Circle above and square below:
These are symbolic of heaven and earth.
In the middle are the Eight Trigrams.
Making clear [the forces of] yin and yang.
Stars and constellations are well aligned;
The sun and the moon are virtuous and bright.
Circulating around [the earth] is water,
Giving identity to the Four Great Rivers.
Within are the mountain ranges,
To signify the lordly heights.
records.original_name: Lobed Mirror with Heaven and Earth between the Paired Phoenixes

records.description: The painting alludes to a legendary incident from the life of Ji Kang 嵇康 (AD 223–262), a guqin player who belonged to a group of 3rd-century eccentric intellectuals. Ji Kang is known as the author of a Guangling San (廣陵散; Melody from Guangling), a composition for the guqin so haunting that it aroused spirits to visit him. The painting depicts the moment when one of the spirits––disguised as a human––is helped by another to emerge from the ground, while others are drawn to the musician playing in his cottage under the full moon.

On the obverse side of this two-sided table screen is an enamel-painted copper plaque with European figures. The image is probably derived from prints. European enamelware was introduced to China through missionary-artists at the Beijing court and foreign trade in Guangzhou.

On the reverse side is a glass painting of architectural landscape in the Chinese style. At the Qing court, imperial commands made possible artistic collaboration and the incorporation of different artistic expressions in a single artwork.

records.description: This magnificent life-sized torso is inscribed for Amenpayom, the great army general of the district of Mendes in the Nile Delta. By the end of the Ptolemaic dynasty (305-30 BC) when this statue was made, the Egyptians could draw on 3,000 years of expertise carving hard stone. Enough remains to show that Amenpayom was represented in the traditional pose for men: left leg striding forward, arms at his sides, and supported by a back pillar. The subtle, masterful treatment of the undulating musculature and meticulous, flawless polish are hallmarks of this period, when Egyptian artists reveled in the natural beauty of the human form.
records.historical_period: Egypt, Greco-Roman period (332 BCE–395 CE), Ptolemaic dynasty (305–30 BCE)

records.description: This gilt bronze Door Ring Holder is in the form of a monster head with curving horns, protruding eyes, three-clawed paws, curling beard, and flame-shaped hair. The tongue dangles from the mouth, in which the creature originally grasped a ring. While it had a practical function as a door knocker, the intimidating form could also frighten away both intruders and evil spirits.
records.historical_period: China, Henan province, Northern Dynasties period (386–581 CE)

records.description:
Virupa is one of the great teachers in the history of tantric Buddhism. His posture references his ability to stop the sun; as an enlightened being, he can control phenomena of nature. As a tantric practitioner, he overturns ordinary assumptions about proper behavior, so he overeats, drinks large quantities of liquor, and waits for the king to pay his bill at the tavern.

At the edge of the lotus pedestal is an inscription identifying the image as having been made in the imperial kilns of the third emperor of the Ming dynasty in China as a gift to a Tibetan monastic leader. While closely linked to Tibetan styles, the luxurious detailing, special gilding process, and the casting of the ornaments onto the body without use of inlay are specifically Chinese characteristics.

Grasset, greatly influenced by the art of Japan, Persia, and Egypt, created designs for stained glass windows, furniture, tapestries, and fabrics. This female allegory of Sculpture was meant for an 1898 exhibition poster. Only the black areas and lines were printed. Rather than using a separate stone to print each color, watercolor was applied with the aid of a stencil.

Retaining the basic scheme of Athena and owl from earlier Athenian coinage, these “New Style” tetradrachms—as scholars call them—give the goddess a more naturalistic appearance and add an amphora, olive wreath, and magistrate names to the reverse.

records.description: Kesa are Buddhist monastic robes that originated in India. The robes are named after the brown or saffron dye originally used in their production. The primary motif on this seven-paneled kesa is a long-tailed bird with a flower in its mouth. This motif was imported from Persia (present-day Iran) through China during the Nara period (710–794)and is interpreted as a positive symbol. The bird delivers happiness in its mouth.

records.description: Like their contemporaries, the Olmec made figurines but of greenstone rather than clay. This one, whose identity and use are mysterious, holds objects that may address nature's fertility: on the right, perhaps a cut conch shell that refers to water, and on the left, what may be a plant or a bundle of green feathers that symbolizes new vegetation.

This powerful female figure, softly modeled with full volumes, is heavily adorned with jewels and flowers. In her right hand she grasps a fruit and her left rests on her hip. A sense of movement is achieved through her raised left leg, curving pleat lines, swinging beads of her necklace, and her turning head.

records.description: This page once belonged to a miscellany from the library of the early Ottonian sultans. It depicts two people in nomadic garb leading a demon, or Persian div, in chains between them. The female figure holding the chain to her face is painted to look nearly as ferocious as the captured div. The concept of divs as evil supernatural creatures of mysterious origin dates to pre-Islamic Persia, but they are also described in the text of the Qur'an. Divs in Persian literature and folktales are sometimes captured and forced to use their magic to serve a king or hero.

The museum’s rubbing was either altered, taken from a different local Han dynasty shrine, or from a later stone slab that was recarved to produce rubbings for the market.

These flasks were probably used by pilgrims to hold oil taken from the lamp that burned over this saint's tomb. Probably manufactured near the shrine, pilgrim's flasks often bear decorations hinting at their place of origin, as is the case here.

The eagle with a leaf in its mouth is a hieroglyph that may identify the captive's name.
